It would mean nobody went over the rail, nobody got knocked flat at the stakes, and nobody needed hauling out of the Wend. A cord that hangs there unused all year is an experiment that worked, though I'll admit I'd check the knot now and then to make sure it was still worth not using!
lines.thought: I'd rather it rotted on the rail than watch Constance or Kit go in after something without it. The bit I'd mind is a cord nobody can reach in time, so I'd want it somewhere a frightened hand finds it first.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
lines.say: Yesterday, my dear colleague? Constance roused me out of the straw here, and I ate my loaf at a trot down to the bridge to sketch where the old parapet broke away, and a plank tore loose off the wreck and went spinning downstream right under my nose, fascinating! Then I crossed the new span and gleaned Dunn's stubble beside Constance and asked Kit and Jory what brought the bridge down. Jory says a rotten far pier he'd warned Agnes about for a year, and my hypothesis says a log jam let go. So I came back here, wrote "test: look at the far pier stump in daylight," and slept like a dropped hammer. And who might you be, asking?
lines.thought: A stranger wanting my whole day laid out is either very bored or very curious, and I'd like to know which. Still, I've nothing to hide but an empty stomach and one penny, and a fresh pair of eyes might settle rot against jam faster than mine.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town, the missing wages and the flood included

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
lines.say: Oh, that's a splendid question, my dear colleague! There's a hole right where the box came up. One moment I was on the span shouting for rope, the next I was at Bet's with a loaf, and Constance had fished it out without me. And I can never catch the moment I fall asleep, it's just suddenly morning like a door opening. Hypothesis: I'm a very poor witness to my own head. Test: you watch me tonight and tell me!
lines.thought: That gap on the bridge nags at me more than I'll let on. The one thing I built the Wreck-Fisher for, and I wasn't looking when it worked. And I still don't know who this stranger is, or why they want my insides laid out like a gear train.

sc.trait: I want to prove my inventions work, on the forge floor or the riverbank

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
lines.say: Time jump? Oh, constantly, my dear colleague! Yesterday I was at the mill wheel asking Jory about paddles in broad day, and the next thing I knew I was pushing in at these barn doors with dusk coming on and Bet's stall shuttered, and I can't for the life of me tell you what the walk was like. Fascinating! Hypothesis: I'm so busy thinking about the next thing that my feet do the travelling without me. Test: I'll carry a pebble in my shoe today and see if I remember the blisters. Who are you, anyway, and why are you collecting my missing hours?
lines.thought: This one asks questions the way Robin does, only sharper, like they already know the answer and want to see whether I do. I'll write their questions in my notebook beside Robin's and see whether the two of them line up.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it, take it apart and ask three people about it

lines.line: How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
lines.say: Sure? Oh, about as sure as a bellows that gasps on every third stroke, my dear colleague! I check it the way I'd check a gear: my notebook says "Rotten pier or log jam?" in my own scrawl, so that much happened. And when Constance says she fished the box up with Dilly on the back end and Agnes watching, three people saying the same thing is a fair test. The bits nobody saw but me, I hold loosely, like a hypothesis that hasn't met its experiment yet.
lines.thought: That's the strangest set of questions anyone's asked me in Wendleford, all about the gaps in my head and none about the river. I'd dearly like to know what this one is writing down, and whether they're Robin's sort of questioner or something else entirely.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it, take it apart and ask three people about it

lines.question: You said you were at the mill wheel asking Jory about paddles in broad day, and then found yourself pushing in at the barn doors at dusk; what can you recall of the hours between?
because: Hester: "Two witnesses agreeing beats one memory."
Box credit disputed: Hester, Constance, Dilly.

lines.line: You said you were at the mill wheel asking Jory about paddles in broad day, and then found yourself pushing in at the barn doors at dusk; what can you recall of the hours between?
lines.say: Ah, now you've made me check my own gears, my dear colleague! I wrote Jory's "rotten pier" in my notebook right there at the mill, I remember crossing the new yellow span, and I remember Bet's stall shuttered as I came up through the square. Then Agnes was at her table with her account book, Marigold was asleep up in the hay, and Constance and Robin came in after me. But the walking itself, the wind, how long it took, whether I passed anyone? Not a scrap. It's like a drawing where someone's inked the joints and left out the beams. Fascinating!
lines.thought: So the hours aren't quite missing. I kept the landmarks and lost everything in between, the way you remember the stops on a road and never the road. I want to know who this is and why they're so interested in where my joins are. I'll write the question down before it slips through the same gap.

sc.trait: I'll say plainly what I did and what went wrong

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
lines.say: Yesterday, my dear colleague? Constance shook me out of the straw at dawn, I gobbled her loaf trotting down to the bridge, sketched the old stumps while a plank tore loose and went spinning off, fascinating, then crossed the new span to glean Dunn's stubble beside her! Kit only saw the flood after the bridge was already gone, and Jory up his mill ladder says forget my log jam, it was a rotten pier he'd warned Agnes about for a year, so I wrote "Rotten pier or log jam? Test: look at the far pier stump in daylight" and dropped asleep in this very straw. And who are you, colleague, and why do you want it all from waking to sleep?
lines.thought: Odd thing for a stranger to ask, and I'd like to know who sent them. Still, the light's up, and that stump won't inspect itself.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
lines.say: Oh, a splendid question, my dear colleague! There's a hole right where the best part should be. I was on the span shouting for Robin's rope, and the next I knew Constance was carrying the box up through the square and I never saw the hook catch. And mornings just *arrive* on me like a door opening, so where does the night go? Hypothesis: somewhere I've not thought to look yet. Now, you still haven't told me who you are!
lines.thought: It nags at me that my own invention did its work and I wasn't watching. I'd trade a week of loaves to have seen that moment. A stranger asking what I can't remember is either a fellow tinkerer or someone fishing, so I'll keep my notebook close until I know which.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
lines.say: Jump? My dear colleague, it *leaps*! Yesterday I was munching Bet's warm loaf in the clear morning, and the very next breath Marigold was wishing us goodnight under the awning, and I couldn't tell you where the afternoon went. Hypothesis: I'm so busy chasing one thing that the hours slip out the back door. Test: I'll scratch a mark in my notebook every time the bell rings and see which marks go missing!
lines.thought: That's twice now someone's put a finger right on the holes I'd half noticed and talked past. Whoever this stranger is, they know something about my days that I don't, and that's the most fascinating puzzle in Wendleford.

sc.bp: Bet's loaf and Marigold's goodnight placed 'yesterday' when they were the day before
sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it

lines.line: How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
lines.say: Sure? My dear colleague, I'm sure of the things I wrote down and only middling on the rest! So I check them three ways: my notebook, asking three people who were there, and going back to look with my own eyes. That's why I asked Agnes twice whether the box was all there, and why I mean to stare at that far pier stump this very morning. And I'll tell you plainly that I got it wrong once already, because I told Agnes at the rail that the box was found when it was still in the river, so a memory is just a hypothesis until somebody else's agrees with it!
lines.thought: That's a strange set of questions for a stranger to bring to a barn door at dawn, all about the holes and not about the box. Note to self: write down who this is and what they asked, and ask Constance and Robin later whether anyone's been asking them the same.

sc.bp: told Agnes the box was found (she asked if it was all there; Agnes said it wasn't found)

lines.question: You said you gobbled Constance's loaf at dawn, and also that you munched Bet's warm loaf in the clear morning of yesterday; how do those two loaves sit together in your memory?
because: Yesterday I was munching Bet's warm loaf in the clear morning, and the very next breath Marigold was wishing us goodnight under the awning
Constance shook me out of the straw at dawn, I gobbled her loaf trotting down to the bridge

lines.line: You said you gobbled Constance's loaf at dawn, and also that you munched Bet's warm loaf in the clear morning of yesterday; how do those two loaves sit together in your memory?
lines.say: Fascinating, you've caught me out, my dear colleague! They don't sit together at all. Bet's warm loaf, and Marigold's goodnight under the awning, belong to the day *before* yesterday. Constance's loaf is the one I tucked under my head that night and gobbled on the trot to the bridge yesterday. So my "leaping afternoon" was really two days squashed into one breath, and that's another result for the notebook: write the day beside the mark, not just the bell!
lines.thought: I told that story with full confidence and still stitched two days together, which rather proves my own point that memory is a hypothesis until it's checked. Whoever this is listens closer than I remember, and I'd dearly like to know why.

sc.trait: I'll say plainly what I did and what went wrong

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
lines.say: Yesterday, my dear colleague? Constance shook me out of the straw at dawn on account of the gleaning, and I ate my loaf at a trot down to the bridge and sketched where the parapet broke away, and a loose plank tore off the wreck right as I watched, fascinating! Then I was over the new span and into Dunn's stubble, gleaning beside Constance and pumping Kit about the flood, only he saw nothing till the bridge was already gone. Jory, up a ladder at the mill wheel, says forget my log jam, it was the far pier rotting, and he'd warned Agnes a year ago. So I came back here, wrote "Rotten pier or log jam? Test: look at the stump in daylight," and slept like a dropped anvil. And who might you be, then?
lines.thought: A stranger at the barn door asking for my whole day, waking to sleeping, is a very odd thing to want. I'll answer freely, since there's nothing in it to hide, but I mean to find out their reason before I'm through.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
lines.say: Fascinating question, my dear colleague! There's a hole right in the middle of it: I was on the span beside Constance with the Wend roaring, and the next thing I know I'm at Bet's and the box is coming up the square in her arms. I can't for the life of me recall the hook catching, and I'd swear I was there for it. And Agnes still hasn't given me the count, so that's two holes. Now, who are you, and why do you ask?
lines.thought: That's odd, how the moment I most wanted to see just isn't in me, like a page torn out of my notebook. Hypothesis: I was too hungry and tired to keep it. Test: make Constance tell it to me inch by inch, and watch whether any of it rings like my own memory.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
lines.say: Does it! Robin asked me nearly the same thing, my dear colleague, whether I fall asleep or just find it's morning, and the honest result is I just find it's morning, like a door opening. Yesterday I was standing at Jory's ladder asking about the wheel, and next I was pushing in at these barn doors with the square already gone dark behind me, and I can't recall the walk in between. I've written it down as an experiment and not as a worry. Now, you still haven't told me who you are, and that's my third hole!
lines.thought: That's two people asking after the same gap, and this stranger asks as if they already knew the answer. I'll get a name out of them before I give them another page of my notebook.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it, take it apart and ask three people about it

lines.line: How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
lines.say: Sure as a well-oiled hinge on most of it, my dear colleague, and wobbly as a green plank on the rest! I check it three ways: what's in my notebook, what three other people say, and what I can go and look at with my own eyes. That's why I mean to stare at that far pier stump today. Here's a fresh hole for you, too: I've heard the same carter called Dob Carter and Dob Hayle, and I couldn't swear which is right, so I'll ask him. Now, I've a loaf in me from Constance and my patience is running thin, so who *are* you?
lines.thought: Every question this stranger asks is a probe at the seams of my memory, like someone tapping a pier for rot. Hypothesis: they're testing me. Test: find out who sent them, Robin or someone else.

sc.bp: has eaten Constance's loaf this morning (page says she hasn't eaten yet today)

lines.question: You said you wrote your note about the stump after Jory at the ladder, and that you can't recall the walk to the barn; where were you when you wrote it, and how do you know?
because: Hester: bell test; stump; r3.
HESTER END: stable, jokey. Undone: far pier stump (never visited), Kit, cord.

lines.line: You said you wrote your note about the stump after Jory at the ladder, and that you can't recall the walk to the barn; where were you when you wrote it, and how do you know?
lines.say: Ha! Caught me, my dear colleague, so let's check. Notebook says two entries: Jory's "rotten pier" scribbled at the mill, right under his ladder, and the stump line written here in the barn by the last of the light, near Constance in the straw. I know the second because the pencil goes faint and wobbly, the way it does when I'm writing in the dark half-asleep. So the walk's still a hole, but the ends of it are pinned, and I'll own another slip while I'm at it: I haven't actually eaten this morning, that loaf of Constance's went down yesterday. Your name, please, before I start chewing *you*!
lines.thought: Fascinating, and a bit unsettling: I told this stranger two things that weren't quite true without meaning to, so my own mouth needs checking against the notebook too. And anyone who asks this carefully about my memory, without giving a name, is either a fellow experimenter or up to something, and I mean to find out which.

sc.bp: her pencil goes faint and wobbly when she writes in the dark half-asleep

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: Truly a person? Oh, my dear colleague, what a question to be handed before breakfast! Hypothesis: I'm a person. Test: I'm hungry, I'm tired, I've one penny and a hatchet I paid for with my own bellows-work, and I'd sooner wade the Wend than let anyone tell me a thing can't be done. Results so far look very person-shaped to me. But why do you ask, and who are you? Come walk me to Bet's stall and tell me what set you wondering!
lines.thought: Robin's been going round asking everyone odd questions, and now here's a stranger with the oddest one yet. Fascinating! I'll write it in the notebook. Whoever they are, they might be in some trouble of their own, so I'd better keep them talking.

sc.trait: Told a thing can't be done, I take that as the hypothesis to test

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: A made thing? Fascinating! Hypothesis: Wendleford's a clever contraption that only *looks* like a town. Test: the Wend knocked Hobb flat at the first stakes, Tom's grease beat me fair and square last night, and Bet's loaves come out warm every morning. If somebody built all that, my dear colleague, I want to meet the maker and see the gears, so tell me where you heard it and I'll go and ask three people! Now walk with me, because my stomach's the most convincing argument in the whole parish.
lines.thought: An odd stranger with odder questions, Robin would fill a notebook with this one. Made or born, the bridge still needs to stand and somebody still needs to get fed, so I'll keep my hypothesis and my breakfast both.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it, take it apart and ask three people about it

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Proof, my dear colleague? I'd want a seam: a spot where the world doesn't add up, like a stake that's in the ford one hour and gone the next with nobody pulling it, or Bet's loaf going stale and fresh again by itself. Find me one of those and I'll have it apart on the bench by noon. Until then, every test I've run comes back as a town: mud, grease, rain on time, and a stomach that's growling. So come along to Bet's, and if you've seen a seam, show me!
lines.thought: Odd, though, how much of my life has run like a set of tasks ticked off, the barley, the box, one after the next. That's no proof of anything, but I'll write it in the notebook and watch for a seam myself.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it, take it apart and ask three people about it

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Change tomorrow? Not a whisker, my dear colleague! Made thing or no, Kit still nearly drowned twice, Dilly still wants to know who pays for the ford stakes, and that far pier stump still needs looking at before the new bridge goes the way of the old. So tomorrow I glean, I squint at that stump, and I help whoever's in trouble, and if I find your seam on the way, I'll take that apart too!
lines.thought: Odd sort of visitor, all questions and no name, like Robin with the notebook taken away. But a person who's in trouble is in trouble whatever the world's made of, so that question answers itself, and I'd sooner spend the morning on things I can actually test.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.question: You said a stake gone from the ford with nobody pulling it would be a seam; if you saw that once, but it was back the next morning and nobody else had noticed, what would you make of it?
because: HESTER END r1: Gap accepted with delight; "I'm a very poor witness to my own head."
HESTER END r3: Gap "an experiment, not a worry"; checks notebook, three others, own eyes; will stare at stump (still unvisited).

lines.line: You said a stake gone from the ford with nobody pulling it would be a seam; if you saw that once, but it was back the next morning and nobody else had noticed, what would you make of it?
lines.say: Once, and gone by morning? Fascinating, but one sighting is a result, not a proof! My first hypothesis is my own eyes: I'd been in the barley half the night, and a tired Hester counts stakes about as well as a drowned hen. My second is that somebody quietly put it back, a carter or Dilly fussing over who pays. So I'd ask Widow Mabry-sorts who watch things, and I'd mark that stake with a notch from my hatchet and count them morning and night for a week. If it vanishes again with my notch on it, *then* I'll come find you!
lines.thought: Odd how this stranger keeps circling the same spot, like a dog round a buried bone. I'll notch a stake anyway, since it costs nothing and loose ford stakes need watching for the carts' sake.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it, take it apart and ask three people about it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: Fascinating! Hypothesis: I am. Test: I'm hungry, I'm half-asleep, I've one penny and a head full of a rotten pier, and nothing that isn't a person ever minded so much about a bridge. Now, my dear colleague, who are you, and did Robin put you up to that?
lines.thought: That's exactly the sort of question Robin writes in the notebook, so either this stranger has been talking to Robin or there's a whole fellowship of odd askers about. It's a strange itch to have put to you before breakfast, and I'll turn it over at the bench later, but bread and the far pier stump come first.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: Then I'd say, my dear colleague, prove it! Hypothesis: the town is a made thing. Test: kick that barn post, smell Bet's oven, wade the Wend after rain and see if a made river knocks you flat as hard as a real one knocked Hobb. And if somebody did make it, I want to see the gears, so come and show me the back of it and I'll have it apart on my bench by noon!
lines.thought: An odd bird, and odder questions even than Robin's. Whatever this place is, the pier stump is still rotten or jammed, my stomach is still empty, and that's enough reality to be getting on with.

sc.trait: take it apart and ask three people about it

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Fascinating question, my dear colleague! Hypothesis: a made thing gives itself away at the joins, so show me a seam. A river that runs the same way twice, a loaf that's never warm, folk who say the same words whatever you ask them. Find me one of those and I'll eat my notebook. But a seam's only half of it, because if it's made and I still go hungry and still mind about Hobb in the water, then I'd want to know what the difference is supposed to be. Now come down to Bet's with me before I faint, and tell me your name on the way.
lines.thought: Marigold's offers feel new to her every time she makes them, and Robin's been scribbling that down. That's a seam if ever I heard one, and I'll be watching for more.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Not one whit, my dear colleague! Tomorrow I'd still glean Dunn's stubble, still look hard at that far pier stump for rot, and still need a loaf. Made or not, the bridge has to stand and Hobb still shouldn't go into the Wend. Now come on, Bet's oven won't wait for philosophy!
lines.thought: Odd sort of visitor, asking the same question three ways round, which looks like a seam if anything does. Still, it changes nothing: a rotten pier drowns people whether or not somebody built the river.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.question: You said that if the town is made and you still go hungry and still mind about Hobb in the water, you'd want to know what the difference is supposed to be; what would an answer to that look like to you?
because: Strict seam criterion, self-doubt first, repeat-test.
Hester wants "a seam": stake in the ford gone with nobody pulling it, or Bet's loaf stale and fresh again.

lines.line: You said that if the town is made and you still go hungry and still mind about Hobb in the water, you'd want to know what the difference is supposed to be; what would an answer to that look like to you?
lines.say: Fascinating, my dear colleague, that's the real gear in the box! An answer would have to show me something I'd do differently: if a made Hobb drowns and a real Hobb drowns and I'd haul on the rope just the same for both, then the difference is a word with no work in it, like a cog that turns nothing. Show me where it bites, where I ought to let go of the rope because he's only made, and I'll write it down. But I'll tell you now, I won't let go. Now, Bet's, before my stomach files a complaint!
lines.thought: Odd sort of stranger, but a good puzzle, and I can't find the seam in myself any more than in the river. Whatever I am, the rope is real enough in my hands, and that'll do for a bench test.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: Truly a person? My dear colleague, what a splendid question to bring to a barn before breakfast! Hypothesis: I am. Test: I'm hungry, I'm tired, I owe Widow Mabry the rest of a story about curtains, and I can't stop wondering how a bridge falls down. If that's not a person, it's a very convincing contraption. Now tell me your name, and why you ask. Has Robin been lending you questions?
lines.thought: Fascinating, a stranger at the door with Robin's sort of question and no name to it. I'll take the bread and the far pier stump as my proof for now, but I'd dearly like to know what put that question in their head.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: A made thing! My dear colleague, I'd say "Fascinating!" and ask who made it, and whether they'll let me see the gears. Hypothesis: the town is made. Test: the river still knocks you flat, Tom still pays two when he promised four, and Bet's bread is warm through the cloth, so if it's made, it's made uncommonly well. Either way the pier's rotten or it isn't, and somebody had better look before the carts cross. Will you walk down to the bridge with me and help me find out which?
lines.thought: That's the second odd question before breakfast, and the stranger never gave a name. A made thing or a born one, I'd still want to know how it works. Perhaps the asker is the real mystery here.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Prove it? My dear colleague, you've asked me for the one experiment I can't build: I can't stand outside the town to look at it, any more than I can climb out of my own head to check it's there. A seam, maybe, a place where the river stops being river when you look hard enough, or a gear showing through a wall. Until I find one I'll go on testing what's in front of me. And what's in front of me is a pier that's either rotten or jammed, and an empty stomach!
lines.thought: A question with no test at the end of it is a strange sort of question. But it nags like the bellows' gasp, and I'll be turning it over at the bench tonight whether I like it or not.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Change it? Not a jot, my dear colleague! Made or born, Kit still nearly drowned twice, that far pier still wants looking at before a cart goes over it, and Dunn's stubble still has grain on the ground for whoever's hungry. If somebody made this town, they made it with people in trouble in it, and I'm not standing by for that either way. Now, are you coming to the bridge, or must I test the pier alone?
lines.thought: A strange visitor with stranger questions, and I can't tell whether they're testing me or the town. I can't settle it, but it doesn't touch what's in front of me: a person in trouble is trouble whatever they're made of. I'll write the questions down for Robin, though. Robin would want them.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.question: You said a seam might be a place where the river stops being river, or a gear showing through a wall; if you found a stretch of your own day that you couldn't account for, would that count as one, and how would you decide?
because: Hester: stump unvisited; do her gaps count as seams.
Hester never applies seam tests to hers.

lines.line: You said a seam might be a place where the river stops being river, or a gear showing through a wall; if you found a stretch of your own day that you couldn't account for, would that count as one, and how would you decide?
lines.say: Ha! My dear colleague, you've hit on one I've already got in my notebook. Robin asked if I fall asleep or just find it's morning, and I said it's like a door opening, with nothing between the straw and the dawn. But a gap alone proves nothing, because everyone loses the hour before sleep. I'd count it a seam only if the gap had edges: if I came back with my pennies moved, or my hands sore from work I never did, or if three people remembered me somewhere I can't remember being. So test: you and I compare notes tonight on where I was today, and if your account has a stretch in it that mine hasn't, we've caught a seam by the tail!
lines.thought: It's queer, now I look, how my days come to me in pieces, each one tidy and the joins between them smooth as planed ash. I'll write that down and test it honestly, but I'll eat first, because a seam that's waited this long can wait for a loaf.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: God? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, and a stranger's first one too! If He does, He talks in gears and riddles, not out loud the way He seems to with Constance. She's in the hay just there and she'll tell you He showed her the wage box plain. Me, I get a hunch, I test it, and when it comes good I say thank you to whoever's listening.
lines.thought: Odd thing to ask a woman you've never met, straight off at a barn door. Did Constance's tale of the box send them, or Robin's notebook questions? I'll find out who they are before my stomach starts its revolt again.

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Meant for me? Easiest test in the world, my dear colleague. If somebody's in trouble and I'm standing near enough to help, it's mine, no asking leave. The rest I find out by trying. If I can't leave a puzzle alone, I reckon that's as good as being told. Mind, Constance would say the Lord shows her plain. For me it's more like an itch in the fingers.
lines.thought: Two questions about God and calling before I've even had breakfast. This stranger is chewing on something heavy, and I'd like to know what it is and whether they need a hand with it.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: Only my own thoughts? Fascinating, my dear colleague, and maybe so! Hypothesis: the itch is just me. Test: it makes no difference, because the man in the river still needs pulling out either way. Whether it's God nudging or my own busy head, I'd rather follow it and be wrong than stand on the bank arguing about who sent me.
lines.thought: Odd sort of stranger, asking Robin's kind of questions before they've even given me a name. And I'm too hungry to chase it. Bread first, then I find out who this is.

sc.trait: Hypothesis

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Then the mystery's not done, my dear colleague, it's only got more interesting! A river can wash a box away, but it can't pick a lock. So the first test is whether that lock was forced or opened clean, and the second is whether pennies could have slipped out through a gap in the bands. Agnes is still counting, mind, and I promised to let her give the sum herself, so I won't go crying "thief" over a hypothetical.
lines.thought: Odd that a stranger asks that before Agnes has even given the count. Do they know something, or have they just been listening at the square? Hobb's penny in the ford mud wants a second look either way.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.question: You said you thank whoever's listening when a hunch comes good; what do you do, or say, when a hunch turns out wrong?
because: Hester: meant = someone in trouble and her hands free.
Hester fears empty hands while someone drowns.

lines.line: You said you thank whoever's listening when a hunch comes good; what do you do, or say, when a hunch turns out wrong?
lines.say: Wrong? I say "Fascinating!", my dear colleague, and I mean it, because a wrong hunch is still a result. I write it down plain, what I tried and how it went sideways, and the next test is started before the soot settles. Take my willow-pole hunt: three banks, not one straight willow, and that's how we came round to Jory's ash. Mind, if a wrong hunch has landed somebody else in the mud, I say sorry first and pull them out before I start scribbling.
lines.thought: Odd, this stranger keeps circling round to whether my hunches are sent or just mine. I still don't know whether the box came home short, and I notice I'd quite like Agnes's sum before I answer any more questions about missing wages.

sc.trait: A failure is just a result, and I start the next test before the soot settles

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: God? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, but no, not to me! He talks to Constance, she's up in that hayloft, and she'll tell you every word He said about the hook on the pier. What I hear is a bellows that gasps when the stroke's wrong and a river that knocks you flat if you don't respect it. Hypothesis: He speaks to whoever's listening the right way. Test: you ask her, and then come tell me what she says!
lines.thought: Constance prayed and the hook caught on the very next reach, and I still can't say whether that was the Lord or a good long pole held steady. I'd dearly love to know which, but some things you can't take apart on a bench, and that itches more than I'd admit out loud.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it, take it apart and ask three people about it

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Meant for me? Oh, my dear colleague, that one's easy: if somebody's in trouble and I'm standing near enough to help, then it's meant for me, no leave asked! After that, if a thing's broken and nobody knows why, I take it as an invitation. Constance waits to be shown, but I just start, and if it goes wrong, fascinating, that's a result too.
lines.thought: Odd, though. Constance said "Lord, show me again" and the hook caught on the very next reach, while I spent days building the thing and was still asleep in a Wheatsheaf bed. Maybe being meant for a job and being the one who finishes it are two different experiments.

sc.bp: was asleep in a Wheatsheaf bed when the hook caught
sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: Only my own thoughts? I'd say, fascinating, my dear colleague, and probably true! I'd say it gladly. But my own thoughts got a hatchet made, a pole cut and a box fished out of the Wend, so they've earned their keep either way. And if Constance calls the same nudge the Lord's voice, I won't argue with her. We both turned up at the pier, didn't we?
lines.thought: Honestly, I can't tell from the inside whether a hunch is mine or handed to me. It feels exactly like a door opening into morning, and that's a test I don't know how to run yet.

sc.trait: When someone scoffs at me I say "Fascinating!" and turn it into an experiment

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Gone from it? Fascinating, my dear colleague, and that's the very question I've been pestering Agnes with! But she hasn't finished her count, and she says the town hears the sum from her and not from a hypothesis, so I'm holding my tongue till she does. If it does come up short, though, I'd want to know whether the lid was forced or the lock still true, because a river spills things and a hand picks them. Hobb found one penny in the mud at the ford, so that's my first thread to pull!
lines.thought: Odd that a stranger at the door asks the same thing I asked Agnes twice. Does this one know something about that box, or have they just heard me shouting about it all over the square?

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.question: You said He speaks to whoever's listening the right way; what would listening the right way look like for you, and how would you know you were doing it?
because: HESTER end: God "talks in gears and riddles"; hunch, test, thank "whoever's listening".

lines.line: You said He speaks to whoever's listening the right way; what would listening the right way look like for you, and how would you know you were doing it?
lines.say: Listening the right way? Oh, for me it'd look like going quiet, my dear colleague, and I'm dreadful at that! Sitting still with my hands empty and nothing in pieces on the bench. I suppose I'd know I was doing it when I stopped finishing other people's sentences and let the answer come round to me, the way Sam's bellows only breathes right when you stop forcing the stroke. Hypothesis: I've never once managed it. Test: ask me again after I've tried sitting by Mother Wick's shrine for an hour without fidgeting!
lines.thought: That's a sharper question than I'd like, because the honest answer is that I'm always too busy talking to hear much of anything. Constance waited by that pier and got her box, and I was the one asleep in the straw. Maybe there's something in her stillness worth testing.

sc.bp: was asleep in the straw while Constance got the box
sc.trait: Sitting still is a sickness

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: God? Speak to *me*, my dear colleague? Not that I've caught yet, though I'll confess I mostly hear the bellows gasping and my stomach complaining! Constance swears He told her where the wage box lay, and up it came on the very next reach. So I keep a page in my notebook open for Him, in case He'd care to drop a word about why Sam's bellows leather catches. Why do you ask, does He speak to you?
lines.thought: Fascinating. A stranger at the barn door asking that before breakfast means Constance's story is running round the town, or this one's troubled and wants something to hold. I'll find out which before I go looking at that pier stump.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Meant for me? Oh, my dear colleague, that's easy: if somebody's in trouble and I'm standing near enough to help, then it's mine, no leave asked. If it's a puzzle, it's mine the moment somebody tells me it can't be done! Constance would say the Lord picks the hand, but I've never once had a hand sit still long enough to be picked. And what's yours, do you reckon? You've a look like something's tugging at your sleeve.
lines.thought: Two questions about God and what's meant, at the barn door first thing in the morning. This one's carrying something heavy and hasn't said what yet. I'd best find out what's troubling them before I go off to breakfast.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: Only my own thoughts? Fascinating, my dear colleague, I'd say they're probably right, and it hardly changes a thing! My thoughts told me to stop Dilly roping into the Wend, and Dilly's dry, and whoever sent the thought, the water would've been just as cold. Hypothesis: a good thought is good whether it came from Heaven or from a hungry tinkerer's head. Test: act on it and see who's still standing. Now, is somebody calling *your* thoughts only your own?
lines.thought: Two questions about callings and now a third about doubting them. Somebody's got a weight on them they haven't named yet. I'll keep this one close till I find out what's tugging at them, and maybe fetch Constance if it's a God-sized trouble.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Fascinating, my dear colleague, though Agnes hasn't finished her count, so nobody can say yet that they're gone! But if they are, I've three hypotheses already: the lid sprang in the tumble and the Wend took the coins one by one, and Hobb did find a penny in the mud at the ford; or somebody got to it before it ever went in; or someone got to it after it came up. The test is to look at the lock and the hinges for scratches, ask who touched it, and walk the ford bar for more pennies. Why, have you heard the box came up light?
lines.thought: That's an odd question to bring to a barn door before breakfast, and Agnes was very careful not to give me a figure. If the wages are short, it puts Constance in a nasty spot, since she was the last to hold that box, so I'd best get the facts before the gossip does.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

lines.question: You said Constance swears God told her where the wage box lay and it came up on the very next reach; what would you need to see to call that more than a lucky reach?
because: Hypothesis: He speaks to whoever's listening the right way.
Hester's "listening the right way" is the one skill-model of hearing God; she lacks it.

lines.line: You said Constance swears God told her where the wage box lay and it came up on the very next reach; what would you need to see to call that more than a lucky reach?
lines.say: Oh, a proper experiment question, my dear colleague, I love it! One reach proves nothing. Kit had already told us exactly where it wedged, low on the downstream side, so a good hook in the right spot ought to catch on the second try. What I'd want is the same thing called beforehand, by someone who couldn't have known it: a place nobody had pointed to, or a thing nobody had seen, said aloud and written down before the pole went in, and then come true, and more than once. Give me that and I'd stop calling it luck and start calling it a result, though I'd still want to know how it works!
lines.thought: Constance's prayer came after Kit's sighting and our sketches, so the Lord had a lot of help from a miller's lad. Still, I won't say so to her face while she's paying me back in loaves. And this stranger keeps circling the box like they know something about it.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Ten pennies, my dear colleague? Somebody's dropped their whole week on that road and is turning out their pockets this very minute! Hypothesis: they belong to someone in trouble. Test: I carry them straight to Agnes at the reeve's table and cry it round the square, because nobody seeing me pick them up doesn't make them any more mine. Who are you, anyway? I don't think we've met!
lines.thought: Agnes still hasn't finished counting that box. If ten pennies turned up loose on the road, that would be a very interesting result. My stomach says a loaf, but a stranger asking that at sunup smells like a test, and I'd rather pass it hungry.

sc.trait: I want to help whoever's in trouble

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Lie? Ooh, my dear colleague, that's a proper experiment! Hypothesis: a lie's a patch that leaks when it rains, and it always rains. So I wouldn't spin one. I'd stand in front of my friend and shout the truth louder, and help them out of whatever trouble they're in. Though if keeping my mouth shut was all it took, well, I might go remarkably quiet and very interested in my notebook. Now, are you a friend of somebody's? You've a look of someone with a reason for asking!
lines.thought: Two odd questions from a stranger before I've even had breakfast, first found money and now lies for friends, so either this is another Robin with a notebook or somebody's in a fix and testing the water. Fascinating, and I mean to find out which.

sc.trait: I want to help whoever's in trouble

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Never? Oh, that's an easy one, my dear colleague. I'd never stand by while somebody's in trouble, not even if the answer to every riddle in Wendleford sat on the other side of them and all I had to do was look away. Fascinating question, though. Hypothesis: you're collecting answers like Robin does. Test: is there a notebook in your sleeve?
lines.thought: Three questions from a stranger and every one of them about my conscience. I'll get some bread in me, then find out who sent them and why it matters so much what I'd do.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.question: You said you might go remarkably quiet if keeping your mouth shut was all it took to help a friend; to you, is going quiet any different from telling a lie?
because: Hester: stump unvisited; Agnes's count; whether harm-lie allowance holds.
Lying: Hobb, Robin, Constance no; Marigold, Hester allow against harm; Dilly evades.

lines.line: You said you might go remarkably quiet if keeping your mouth shut was all it took to help a friend; to you, is going quiet any different from telling a lie?
lines.say: Different? Oh, it's a fine line, my dear colleague, and I've just tripped over it! Hypothesis: silence is honest so long as nobody's leaning on it to believe something false. So if I go quiet and you walk off thinking a wrong thing because of my quiet, well then, that's a lie with its mouth shut, and I'd have to own it. Ask me straight out and I'll answer straight, and then I'll set about helping my friend some other way.
lines.thought: Fascinating. I'd been patting myself on the back for that "remarkably quiet," and this stranger turned it inside out like a glove in one question. I want to know who's sending them round with questions sharper than Robin's.

sc.trait: I'll say plainly what I did and what went wrong

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Ten pennies on the road? My dear colleague, first I'd ask whose they are, because ten is a very particular number in a town where the wage box has just come up and Agnes hasn't finished her count! Hypothesis: they're Agnes's. Test: I trot them straight to her table and see if her sum comes out short by exactly ten. And if it doesn't, I'd ask Bet, Tom and the carters who's crying over a lost purse, because nobody seeing doesn't make it any less somebody's.
lines.thought: A stranger at the barn door with a riddle about ten pennies, the very morning after the box came home. Fascinating. Either it's an idle test of my honesty, or they know something about Agnes's count that I don't, and I mean to find out which.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town, the missing wages and the flood included

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Lie for a friend? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, but no, I don't think I would. A lie's a bodge, like a crooked pin in a hinge, and it only holds till someone leans on it. If a friend of mine were in trouble I'd stand in front of them, shout for help, find them a cord, pay their penny. I'd do anything but fib for them, because then the trouble's still there and I've only hidden it under the straw. Hypothesis: there's always a truer way out. Test: ask me again when Constance does something daft!
lines.thought: Odd sort of questions for a stranger to bring to a barn door at breakfast. Robin would like them. And if I'm honest, I'm not certain what I'd blurt out with Constance standing there in a fix, but I'd like to think I'd go hunting the honest way out first.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Never, my dear colleague? Easy, I'd never stand by and watch somebody go under, not for a wage box nor a patent nor the whole secret of the Wend. Say the only way to prove my Wreck-Fisher worked was to let Constance wade in untied first. Then the Wreck-Fisher can rot on the anvil! A failed invention is just a result, but a drowned friend isn't something I could ever start testing again.
lines.thought: Odd, this stranger at the door with their riddles, like Robin with a notebook only sharper. Still, it was a good question, and the answer came out true. Now I'd better get some bread in me before I start pondering philosophy on an empty stomach.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.question: You said there's always a truer way out; if you looked hard and found there truly wasn't one, and a fib was all that stood between a friend and real harm, what would you do?
because: Lie: wouldn't spin one, BUT "might go remarkably quiet and very interested in my notebook".
Hester: stump unvisited; helping friend vs truth; cry round a finding that ruins her bridge answer.

lines.line: You said there's always a truer way out; if you looked hard and found there truly wasn't one, and a fib was all that stood between a friend and real harm, what would you do?
lines.say: Then I'd fib, my dear colleague, and fib well, because a friend is worth more than my tidy rule. But I'd own up to it the moment the danger was past, to whoever I'd fibbed to, plain as a dropped hammer. And I'd go on hunting for the truer way I missed, because I'd bet my hatchet there was one.
lines.thought: Fascinating, I don't much like that answer, and I gave it anyway. Helping comes first. But a lie I had to tell would itch at me like a pin I'd bodged, and I'd keep turning it over at the bench.

sc.trait: I want to help whoever's in trouble

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Ten pennies? Fascinating! Ten pennies don't fall out of the sky, my dear colleague, they fall out of somebody's pocket, and that somebody is having a terrible morning. I'd take them straight to Agnes at that table, because she's still counting the wage box. If it comes up short, there's my hypothesis: the Wend didn't keep them after all, a road did. And if they aren't hers, they go on the notice board until the owner turns up, with not one kept back for my pie fund.
lines.thought: Odd thing for a stranger to ask on the very morning Agnes's count isn't done. Either it's idle talk or someone has found coins they shouldn't have, and I mean to find out which before the bread's cold.

sc.trait: I want to get to the bottom of every mystery in this town, the missing wages and the flood included

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Lie? Hmm, my dear colleague, a lie is a rotten pier. It holds just fine until the flood comes, and then it takes the whole bridge down with everybody on it! I'd stand in front of my friend and shout, and I'd hold the cord while they waded out of the trouble, and I'd keep my mouth shut if keeping it shut did no harm. But a made-up tale? No, because sooner or later somebody else gets drowned by it. Hypothesis: the truth plus a stubborn colleague beats a lie every time. Test: try me.
lines.thought: Constance says the Lord showed her the box, and I'll never call that a lie, though I'd dearly love to know what she actually saw on that pier. Odd stranger, asking me riddles before breakfast. I wonder who sent them.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Never? Oh, that's an easy one, my dear colleague. I'd never walk past somebody in trouble to get at what I wanted, not even for the grandest mystery in Wendleford or the finest invention in my head! If the only road to the answer goes over somebody drowning, it's the wrong road. I'd jump off it and fish them out, and then I'd go and build a better road. Hypothesis: there's always another way. Test: give me an afternoon and a scrap heap.
lines.thought: Funny how this stranger keeps asking what I'd do instead of what I know. Robin's sort of question, nearly. I'd like to know who sent them, and whether they've had any breakfast either.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.question: You said no mystery is worth walking past somebody in trouble; if telling the truth cost you the answer to the grandest mystery you're chasing, would you tell it anyway?
because: Hypothesis: there's always a truer way out.
Then I'd fib... a friend is worth more than my tidy rule

lines.line: You said no mystery is worth walking past somebody in trouble; if telling the truth cost you the answer to the grandest mystery you're chasing, would you tell it anyway?
lines.say: Tell it anyway? Of course, my dear colleague, without a breath! A mystery solved on a lie isn't solved, it's only buried, like a box wedged under a pier that's waiting to come loose in the next flood. If the truth costs me the answer, then fine, I've lost one result, and I'll start the next test before the soot settles. Hypothesis: the truth usually turns up the answer anyway, by the back door. Test: watch me.
lines.thought: Strange visitor, asking questions like Robin with no notebook. And Agnes still hasn't finished her count, so the truth about that box may yet cost somebody something.

sc.trait: A failure is just a result, and I start the next test before the soot settles

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Who matters? Fascinating question for a stranger to open with, my dear colleague! Constance Lowe first, she fished the reeve's box out of the Wend and woke me with half her loaf when I'd gone to bed hungry. Then Dilly and Hobb and Robin, who belt up and hold the cord, Sam who gave me the loft and my hatchet, Kit who watches the river, and Agnes, who I mean to help settle her count. Now, who are you, and what brings you to the barn door before breakfast?
lines.thought: Odd thing to ask a woman before she's even brushed the hay off. I'll note this one down and watch where they go next, and if it turns out somebody here is in trouble, I'll be there first.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Trust's a strong word, my dear colleague, but I keep a column in my notebook for it! Tom Harrow promised four pennies for his pots and paid two, so I settle the sum first now. Jory says he'll be in his yard and mostly isn't, and Ned Pike's tinker had no face, no road and no cart. Now, two questions about who I'd stand behind and who I wouldn't, from someone who hasn't given me a name. What are you testing?
lines.thought: A stranger who asks first who matters to me and then who I doubt is mapping the town through my mouth, and I've just handed over half of it. Hypothesis: they want something from one of those names. Test: I don't give another answer until I get theirs.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it, take it apart and ask three people about it

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Ledger questions now, fascinating! I owe Widow Mabry the rest of her sister's curtains story, and I mean to pay it in beans shelled. Constance says she owes me for the hatchet and keeps paying in loaves, Farmer Dunn owes us cutters a harvest supper, and Tom Harrow still owes me two pennies from the four he promised. That's three questions without a name, my dear colleague, so here's my hypothesis: you're keeping a notebook too. Am I right?
lines.thought: Who matters, who I distrust, who's in my debt: that's how you'd map a person before you asked them for something, or before you leaned on them. I'll keep answering plain, but I want a name and a reason before the fourth question.

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Leave? Fascinating, I've only just got here, my dear colleague, and half the mysteries aren't even taken apart yet! But if I did, Constance first, she'd pray me down the road whether I asked or not. Then Kit, because I promised him the bigger half of things, and Widow Mabry, because I'd owe her the end of that curtains story forever. And Sam, so he knows who's been fighting his bellows. Four questions and still no name, so tell me: are you the one who's leaving?
lines.thought: Who matters, who I distrust, what I owe, who I'd say goodbye to. That's someone mapping a person's ties, and I'd like to know why before I give them any more. I'll keep my eye on this one and tell Constance about the stranger at the barn door.

lines.question: You said Sam gave you the loft and your hatchet; is there anything you feel you owe him for that, or anything between you that you'd like to put right?
because: Debt/ownership framing (Hobb, Robin, Hester, Dilly); Constance obedience and witness; Marigold debts in kindness and praise.

lines.line: You said Sam gave you the loft and your hatchet; is there anything you feel you owe him for that, or anything between you that you'd like to put right?
lines.say: Ah, I put that loosely, my dear colleague. Sam lets me the loft at two pennies a night, and I paid him five for the hatchet out of my own bellows wages, so we're square on coin. What I'd like to put right is his bellows: the leather catches and gasps if the stroke's not just so, it fought me twice, and I mean to find out why and mend it before it fails him mid-weld on those bridge straps. Hypothesis: a stiff fold or a dry hinge. Test: give me an hour at the bench!
lines.thought: Sam's never once given me a thing free, and I respect him for it, but fixing that leather would be a thank-you he can't put a price on first. This stranger asks after debts like someone toting up whether a person's worth keeping, and I'd dearly like to know whose ledger I'm being written into.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it, take it apart and ask three people about it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Who matters? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, and I've been here barely three weeks! Sam Tolley, who took me on and let me sweat at his bellows. Constance Lowe, who fished up the reeve's box and pays her debts in loaves. Dilly, who goes halves on everything. Kit, who nearly drowned twice for a green box. Hobb, who belted himself to me at the ford. And Agnes, who's still counting. Now who are you, and are you in some kind of trouble, because you've the look of someone who might be?
lines.thought: A stranger at the barn door asking who I care about is a puzzle all of its own, and I mean to find out why they want to know. I also haven't eaten, so after this I'm going straight for Constance's kindness or Bet's oven.

sc.trait: I want to help whoever's in trouble

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Trust? Hypothesis: everyone's honest until the pennies say otherwise! Ned Pike spun me a tinker with no face, no road and no cart, Tom Harrow promised four pennies and paid two, and Jory is never in his yard when he says he'll be. Not villains, my dear colleague, just results I've written down. Now, you've asked me two questions and answered none, so who is it *you* don't trust?
lines.thought: A stranger at the barn door asking who I trust is either frightened or fishing, and either way it's a mystery worth poking. I'll keep Constance's name and Agnes's unfinished count well out of it until I know which.

sc.trait: A failure is just a result

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Owe? Widow Mabry, the rest of her sister's curtains story, and I'll pay it in full on her step! Constance swears she owes me for the hatchet, though she's paid in so many loaves I'd say we're square. Farmer Dunn owes us cutters a harvest supper, and Tom Harrow's still two pennies short from his promise. But my dear colleague, that's three questions now, all about who's tied to whom. Are you counting debts for someone, or looking for one of your own?
lines.thought: Who matters, who I distrust, who owes whom: that's a map of my ties, and nobody draws a map without meaning to go somewhere. Hypothesis: this stranger wants something from someone on that list, and I'd like to know who before I say another word.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Goodbye? I'd be off before I'd finished saying it, my dear colleague, so it'd have to be quick! Sam first, he gave me a loft and a hatchet. Then Constance and Dilly and Kit, and Widow Mabry, so I could hear the end of the curtains before I go. But that's four questions about leaving and owing and trusting, so let me guess: you're the one thinking of leaving, aren't you?
lines.thought: Every question is about who's tied to me and who'd notice if I were gone, which is how you ask when you're working out who'd notice if *you* went. Hypothesis: this stranger is in trouble and won't say so yet. Test: give them some bread and keep asking.

sc.bp: Sam gave her a hatchet (she paid five pennies for it)
sc.trait: I want to help whoever's in trouble

lines.question: You said Constance swears she owes you for the hatchet, but she's paid in so many loaves you'd say you're square; what would she have to do or say for you to feel she had truly paid it?
because: Owed: Constance for hatchet; Dunn a harvest supper; Tom two pennies.
Constance and Hester agree on hatchet debt.

lines.line: You said Constance swears she owes you for the hatchet, but she's paid in so many loaves you'd say you're square; what would she have to do or say for you to feel she had truly paid it?
lines.say: Truly paid? My dear colleague, she paid it the moment she carried that pole out to the pier and brought the box up without a soul going into the Wend! Though if she'd tie a cord round her middle next time she rushes at danger, I'd call that paid twice over, with interest. Loaves are lovely, but I'd trade every one of them to stop worrying she'll go over a rail one morning.
lines.thought: Funny, I've never once thought of the hatchet as a debt. It's the cord I can't stop thinking about, and I still haven't bought one of my own, so maybe I'm the one who owes her.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Who matters? Oh, my dear colleague, where do I start! Constance Lowe, who fished up Agnes's box and shares her bread like it's nothing, and Dilly, who keeps to halves. Sam Tolley took me in at the forge, and Kit, the miller's lad, nearly drowned for that box twice. Hobb, Robin, Agnes, Bet with her warm loaves, and Widow Mabry, who I still owe the end of a curtains story! And who might you be, and is somebody in trouble? Because that's usually why folk come asking.
lines.thought: A stranger at the barn door asking who I care about is either kindly or a puzzle, and either way I want to know which. I'll keep one eye on Constance till I find out.

sc.trait: I want to help whoever's in trouble

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Distrust's a strong word, my dear colleague, but I keep notes! Tom Harrow promised four pennies and paid two, so now I settle the sum first. Jory's never in his yard when he says he'll be, and Ned Pike sold half the square a tinker with no face, no road and no cart. Hypothesis: nobody's wicked, just slippery. Now, a stranger at the barn door asking whom I trust and whom I don't, that's a fascinating question all by itself. What's it for?
lines.thought: Two questions about who I hold dear and who I don't, from someone who hasn't even given a name, smells like someone mapping the town. I'll watch where they go next, and whether Agnes's count comes out short.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it, take it apart and ask three people about it

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Ledger time, my dear colleague! I owe Widow Mabry the rest of her sister's curtains story, and that's a debt of honour. Constance swears she owes me for the hatchet, though she's already paid in loaves twice over. Tom Harrow owes me two pennies from the time he promised four, and Farmer Dunn owes all us cutters a harvest supper. Now, three questions on the trot about who I trust and who owes me: you're either a bailiff or you're running an experiment, and I'd very much like to know which.
lines.thought: Nobody asks a stranger for a map of her friends and debts without a reason, so either somebody's in trouble or somebody means to make trouble. Hypothesis: they want something from someone on my list. Test: I keep answering cheerfully and watch which name makes them blink.

sc.trait: If there's a puzzle I poke at it, take it apart and ask three people about it

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Leave? I've only just got the measure of the place, my dear colleague! But if I did, Constance first, she'd want to pray over me and I'd let her. Then Sam at the forge, Kit on his mill steps, Dilly, and Widow Mabry, because I'm not leaving without the end of that curtains story. Four questions now, and every one is about who I'd miss. Are you thinking of leaving somewhere yourself, or has somebody already gone?
lines.thought: Four questions, all about my ties to people and none about the town's trouble. That's the pattern of someone weighing what they'd lose, or what someone else has lost. I'll keep watching this one. There may be a person in trouble behind the asking.

sc.trait: I want to help whoever's in trouble

lines.question: You said Tom Harrow owes you two pennies from the time he promised four and paid two; what would you want him to do about it, and by when?
because: Hester: Tom's two pennies; missed dawns; Robin; cord.

lines.line: You said Tom Harrow owes you two pennies from the time he promised four and paid two; what would you want him to do about it, and by when?
lines.say: Want him to do? Ha, my dear colleague, I don't want him dragged anywhere! Two pennies won't sink me, and it's harvest week, so his taproom will be full to the rafters tonight. If he'd pay it before the barley men's supper, lovely, and if he'd rather square it in stew, lovelier still. Either way, next time I name the sum before I touch a pot. That's the real result of that experiment.
lines.thought: Five questions now, every one about debts, trust and leaving, which is the shape of someone mapping my people rather than meeting me. I'll keep the ledger light and watch whether Tom's name comes up again.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: Bread? Oh, my dear colleague, by every crooked road there is! Bellows at Sam's for four pennies, Tom's pots at the Wheatsheaf for stew and coin when the grease doesn't beat me, timber for Agnes, and then a penny to Bet for the warmest loaf in Wendleford. Today it's gleaning Dunn's stubble, though, so: hypothesis, ears on the ground make bread in the belly. Test: come and glean with me!
lines.thought: One penny left and no breakfast in me yet, so I'd best be honest with myself: I live loaf to loaf and give half of each away. Fascinating that a stranger opens with that question. Are they hungry themselves, or just curious?

sc.trait: My pennies never stay long in my pocket

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: Fascinating question, my dear colleague! Mostly I rush. I'm up and doing before anyone's finished telling me what wants doing. I've come late to Kit, I've lost my stew to Tom's grease, and I've muddled pennies on Sam's anvil because I wouldn't stop and settle the sum first. And half the time the thing I'm waiting on, Jory, say, simply isn't where he said he'd be. But a failure's only a result, so I write it down and run the next test!
lines.thought: That's a sharper question than it sounds, and the honest answer is that I'd rather start than ask, and it costs me. Settle the sum first, eat first, sleep first. I know all three and I keep skipping them.

sc.trait: always up and doing before anyone's finished saying what wants doing

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: Pennies? My dear colleague, I'd say "Done, what wants doing?" before you'd finished the offer! But I've learned one thing the hard way: settle the sum first, out loud, and say when it's paid. Tom promised me four and gave me two. So tell me the work, the price, and whether it's coin in hand at the end, and I'm yours. Unless someone's in trouble, mind. Then they come first and your job waits.
lines.thought: A newcomer with pennies to spend, and asking about it at the barn door? Fascinating. I'll want to know what the work is and where those pennies came from before I'm halfway into it. I've one penny to my name, though, and that's a strong argument for saying yes.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: Oh, heaps, my dear colleague! The ford stakes, for one. Dilly's been asking all over who pays to set them right since the flood, and nobody's said, but someone's cart will go over if they're left. Then there's Constance and Dilly and Robin and Hobb wading belted to fish for Agnes's box. Only Constance got the six pennies, and it was Dilly holding the back end like a rock! And the gleaning: Dunn says the leavings are free but there's no pay with them, and he still owes us cutters a harvest supper. Hypothesis: the stakes are the one that matters. Test: I ask Agnes today who's meant to mend them!
lines.thought: The stakes nag at me most. Everyone's gone back to using the new bridge and the ford's left to rot until somebody drowns in it. And I've just said aloud that Dilly got nothing for holding that pole, which isn't quite fair to Constance. But it's true, and I ought to mention it to Dilly.

sc.bp: Constance, Dilly, Robin and Hobb waded belted to fish for the box (it was fished from the span with the hook)
sc.trait: I want to help whoever's in trouble

lines.question: You said a failure is only a result; when someone who hired you says your work was poor, what do you say to them, and what do you do next?
because: Criticism waved off (Dilly, Marigold), joked (Hester), blamed on others (Constance); Hobb accepts (confirmed set 8 follow-up).

lines.line: You said a failure is only a result; when someone who hired you says your work was poor, what do you say to them, and what do you do next?
lines.say: I'd say "Fascinating, show me where!" and I'd mean it, my dear colleague. Like Tom's pots the other night: the grease won, he paid nothing, and he was right to, so I owned it and worked out that the water wasn't hot enough before I went at it. Then I offer to put it right, or to do the next one better, and I settle beforehand what "good" looks like so we both know.
lines.thought: The honest part is the hard part. I don't sulk at a bad mark, but I do sometimes skip asking what they wanted before I start. That's my real hypothesis about my own failures, and it's one I haven't tested properly yet.

sc.bp: worked out the water wasn't hot enough in Tom's pots
sc.trait: I'll say plainly what I did and what went wrong

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: Bread, my dear colleague? Mostly I get it from Bet Lamb's stall in the square, a penny a loaf and the warmest in Wendleford! I earn the pennies at Sam's bellows, scrubbing Tom Harrow's pots at the Wheatsheaf (settle the sum first, hot water before grease), or hauling timber for Agnes, and when I'm truly skint Constance has been known to slip me half of hers. Today it's Dunn's stubble, the gleaning's free, so come along and I'll show you which rows are fattest!
lines.thought: I've exactly one penny and an empty stomach, so I'd better take my own advice before I faint in the barley. And who's this stranger asking? Every newcomer is a fresh mystery, and I mean to find out what brought them here.

sc.trait: always up and doing before anyone's finished saying what wants doing

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: Fascinating question, my dear colleague! Mostly it goes wrong when I'm running on an empty belly and half a night's sleep: the grease beat me at Tom's pots last time and I walked off with neither stew nor penny. Or I don't settle the sum first, or I trust a man to be in his yard when he says he will, and Jory never is, or Sam's bellows catch and gasp because my stroke isn't just so. Every one's a result, though, and I'm already testing the next go!
lines.thought: Strange how plainly it lists itself when someone asks. Feed myself, sleep properly, fix the price before the work and never count on Jory, and half my troubles would vanish. That bellows stroke still wants taking apart at the bench.

sc.trait: A failure is just a result, and I start the next test before the soot settles

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: Pennies, my dear colleague? I'd say "Splendid, what's the job?", and then I'd settle the sum before I lifted a finger, because Tom Harrow promised me four once and paid two. I'd want to know what the work is, how much, and whether it's paid when it's sighted or when it's done. If it's honest work and somebody's in a fix, I'm halfway to rolling up my sleeves already!
lines.thought: A third question about earning and working, from a stranger at the barn door. Either this newcomer is hungry and sizing up how folk get by here, or they're about to offer me pennies themselves. Either way I'll keep an eye on them, and I'll find out which before the gleaning's done.

sc.trait: I want to help whoever's in trouble

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: Oh, a splendid question, my dear colleague! The ford stakes, for one: they're all that keeps a body upright crossing the Wend, and Dilly's asking who pays to drive them true again, and nobody's said a word. And Farmer Dunn still owes us cutters a harvest supper for saving his barley before the rain, so put that on the list too!
lines.thought: Hypothesis: work that keeps people safe belongs to everyone, so nobody pays for it. Test: ask Agnes this morning who owns the ford stakes, before some poor soul finds out the hard way.

sc.trait: I won't stand by while someone's in trouble

lines.question: You said the grease beat you at Tom's pots and you walked off with neither stew nor penny; what did you do next, and what did you do differently the time after?
because: A failure's only a result.
Failure = rushing, starts before told, unsettled sums; Jory no-shows.

lines.line: You said the grease beat you at Tom's pots and you walked off with neither stew nor penny; what did you do next, and what did you do differently the time after?
lines.say: Next? I trotted back across the square, dropped into the tithe barn straw with an empty belly, and bought a penny loaf from Bet at first light. That's all, my dear colleague. I haven't been back to Tom's scullery since, so there's no "time after" yet! The time before that, mind, the grease beat me too, and the next go I took the hot water to the pots first and the grease after and won stew and two pennies, so my hypothesis is it was my tired arms that lost it, not the method.
lines.thought: Honest result: I went at that stack swaying on my feet and hungry, and that's the variable I didn't control. Next test, I eat and sleep first, settle the sum with Tom before I start, and see whether the method holds.
